questions.question: What are the core concepts in Spring Batch — Job, Step, Chunk, and Tasklet — and how do they relate to each other?
questions.title: Spring Batch Core Concepts: Job, Step, Chunk, and Tasklet
questions.direct_answer: A **Job** is the top-level container representing an entire batch process, composed of one or more **Steps** executed in sequence or conditionally. Each Step follows either a **chunk-oriented model** (read-process-write in fixed-size chunks inside one transaction) or a **Tasklet model** (a single custom unit of work). The **JobRepository** persists every JobInstance, JobExecution, and StepExecution to a relational database, which is what enables restartability, audit trails, and skip/retry tracking — features that distinguish Spring Batch from a hand-rolled batch loop.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands Spring Batch's execution model and the JobRepository persistence layer before writing any code
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing Tasklet with Chunk — candidates often think Tasklet is just a simpler Step, not realizing they are mutually exclusive execution strategies within a Step
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention JobRepository, JobInstance vs JobExecution, and StepExecution as the persistence layer that enables restartability — most candidates skip this entirely

sections.title: Spring Batch's Chunk Model Is a Specific Transaction Boundary Design — Not Just `Process in Groups`
sections.content:
Spring Batch was designed for one problem: **processing millions of records reliably**, with the ability to recover from failures without reprocessing everything. The entire domain model — Job, Step, Chunk, Tasklet, JobRepository — exists to satisfy that constraint.

A **Job** is the top-level unit of work — `process today's orders`, `generate monthly invoices`.
- A Job is composed of **Steps**, each doing one discrete piece.
- Each Step chooses one of two **mutually exclusive** execution strategies.
- **Chunk-oriented processing** is the standard model: read N items → process each → write all N in a single transaction.
- The chunk size is the commit interval.
- If the job fails at item 7001 with chunk size 100, restart resumes at item 7001, not item 1.

**Tasklet** is for everything that isn't record-by-record processing: downloading a file, sending an email, truncating a staging table, calling a stored procedure.
- A Tasklet returns `RepeatStatus.FINISHED` from a single `execute()` method.
- Spring Batch persists every execution to a **JobRepository** backed by a relational database.
- Without JobRepository, you get no restart, no audit, no idempotency protection — which is why Spring Batch suits production financial and operational batch processing where a hand-rolled `for` loop with batch insert does not.

sections.title: The Job → Step → (Chunk or Tasklet) Hierarchy
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
    job["Job (orderImportJob)"]
    job --> step1["Step 1: validateInput"]
    job --> step2["Step 2: importOrders"]
    job --> step3["Step 3: notifyResult"]
    step1 --> taskletA["Tasklet (single execute)"]
    step2 --> chunk["Chunk-Oriented"]
    step3 --> taskletB["Tasklet (single execute)"]
    chunk --> reader["ItemReader.read x N"]
    chunk --> processor["ItemProcessor.process"]
    chunk --> writer["ItemWriter.write (chunk)"]
    chunk --> commit["Transaction commit per chunk"]
    job -.persists.-> repo[("JobRepository (BATCH_* tables)")]
    step1 -.persists.-> repo
    step2 -.persists.-> repo
    step3 -.persists.-> repo
    repo --> instance["JobInstance = Job name + JobParameters"]
    repo --> execution["JobExecution = one run attempt"]
    repo --> stepExec["StepExecution = per-step state + ExecutionContext"]
```

sections.title: The Chunk Transaction Boundary — Why Write Failures Are Different From Read Failures
sections.content:
Understanding the chunk transaction boundary explains most Spring Batch debugging. Each chunk runs inside a **single transaction** spanning the entire read-process-write cycle for those N items.

**Read phase mechanics**
- `ItemReader.read()` is called repeatedly until chunk size is reached or `null` is returned
- Read errors are handled per item via skip/retry policies
- Read failures don't roll back the chunk transaction — they happen before commit scope

**Process phase mechanics**
- Each item passes through `ItemProcessor.process()` individually
- Returning `null` filters the item out of the chunk silently
- Throwing an exception triggers retry/skip evaluation

**Write phase — the dangerous one**
- The entire chunk's processed items are passed to `ItemWriter.write(Chunk<O> items)` in **one call**
- A write failure rolls back the **entire chunk** — all N items are discarded and reprocessed on restart
- This is why Spring Batch recommends idempotent writers

**Tuning the commit interval**
- Chunk size 1: one transaction per item — safe but slow due to commit overhead
- Chunk size 10,000: failure partway through forces reprocessing thousands of items
- 100-500 items per chunk balances throughput with restart granularity for most workloads

**Why `@StepScope` matters for readers**
- Without `@StepScope`, a singleton reader shared across job executions retains state between runs
- `@StepScope` creates a fresh reader per Step execution — required for parameter injection via `@Value("#{jobParameters['key']}")`

```java
@Bean
@StepScope
public FlatFileItemReader<Order> reader(@Value("#{jobParameters['inputFile']}") String file) {
    return new FlatFileItemReaderBuilder<Order>()
            .name("orderReader")
            .resource(new FileSystemResource(file))
            .delimited()
            .names("id", "customerId", "amount")
            .targetType(Order.class)
            .build();
}
```

sections.title: JobRepository — The Persistence Model That Enables Restart and Audit
sections.content:
When a Job is launched, Spring Batch creates a **JobInstance** identified by `Job name + JobParameters`. If that combination has run before and failed, the existing instance restarts from the last checkpoint.

**Tables Spring Batch ships and writes to**
- `BATCH_JOB_INSTANCE` — one row per logical job run (Job name + parameters)
- `BATCH_JOB_EXECUTION` — one row per attempt at a JobInstance (start time, end time, status)
- `BATCH_JOB_EXECUTION_PARAMS` — parameter values for each execution
- `BATCH_STEP_EXECUTION` — per-step state, including `read_count`, `write_count`, `commit_count`, `rollback_count`
- `BATCH_STEP_EXECUTION_CONTEXT` — serialized ExecutionContext per step (reader position checkpoint)
- `BATCH_JOB_EXECUTION_CONTEXT` — serialized ExecutionContext per job

**Schema scripts ship with Spring Batch**
- `schema-h2.sql`, `schema-mysql.sql`, `schema-postgresql.sql` etc.
- For tests, in-memory H2 with the schema is convenient
- Production must use a persistent database — never the deprecated `MapJobRepositoryFactoryBean`

**Re-running protection**
- If a JobInstance already completed successfully and you launch with the same parameters, Spring Batch throws `JobInstanceAlreadyCompleteException`
- This is intentional — prevents accidental re-processing of completed business data
- To force a fresh run, use `RunIdIncrementer` to add a technical `run.id` parameter

```java
@Bean
public Job orderImportJob(JobRepository repo, Step importStep) {
    return new JobBuilder("orderImportJob", repo)
            .incrementer(new RunIdIncrementer())
            .start(importStep)
            .build();
}
```

**Why this is interview-relevant**
- Most candidates describe Spring Batch as 'processes records in batches' and stop
- The JobRepository is the feature that differentiates Spring Batch from a `for` loop with batch insert
- Without JobRepository persistence: no restart, no audit trail, no idempotency, no observability
- Mentioning this signals you've used it in production rather than just read about it

sections.title: Chunk vs Tasklet — When to Use Each
sections.content:
Chunk and Tasklet are mutually exclusive execution strategies for a Step. Pick based on whether the work is a stream of items or a single discrete operation.

| Aspect | Chunk-Oriented Step | Tasklet Step |
|---|---|---|
| Use case | Read-process-write over a stream | Single discrete operation |
| Transaction scope | One transaction per chunk of N items | One transaction for the whole `execute()` |
| Restart semantics | Resumes at last committed chunk boundary | Re-runs from scratch |
| Skip / retry | Built in via `faultTolerant().skip(...).retry(...)` | Manual — you write the logic |
| Examples | Process 10M orders, import CSV to DB | Truncate staging table, send email, call stored procedure |
| Exit signal | `ItemReader.read()` returns `null` | `RepeatStatus.FINISHED` |

sections.title: When to Choose Chunk, When to Choose Tasklet
sections.content:
**When chunk-oriented helps:**
- The work is a stream of records that can be batched (rows from a table, lines from a file, messages from a queue)
- You need restart from the last committed chunk boundary on failure
- You want skip/retry policies for bad records or transient errors
- Per-item observability matters — `read_count`, `write_count`, `skip_count` in StepExecution

**When Tasklet helps:**
- The work is a single discrete action — truncate a staging table, archive yesterday's files, call a stored procedure
- The action has no natural 'item' to iterate over
- You need full control over a single transaction boundary
- Compensating actions between chunk steps (cleanup, audit row insert)

**Watch for:**
- **Forcing chunk model on non-streaming work** — using a synthetic single-item reader to wrap a procedure call costs you simplicity without benefit
- **Forcing Tasklet on streaming work** — you lose restart, skip, retry, and per-item metrics; you re-implement them poorly by hand
- **Long-running Tasklet without checkpoints** — if a 4-hour Tasklet fails at minute 230, the entire 4 hours re-runs; chunk would resume from the last commit
- **Mixing models in the same Step** — Spring Batch enforces mutual exclusion; the builder API will not let you set both

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Job → Steps → Chunk or Tasklet** — `Job` is the complete batch process; `Step` is one phase; `Chunk` and `Tasklet` are the two execution models for a step.
- **`JobRepository` persists every execution** — stores `JobInstance`, `JobExecution`, `StepExecution` in the database; without it, restart, skip, and retry do not work.
- **Chunk processing is transactional per chunk, not per record** — chunk of 100 items is read, processed, and written inside one transaction; write failure rolls back only that chunk.
- **Tasklet is for single operations** — file cleanup, API calls, DDL, stored procedures; implement `Tasklet` and return `RepeatStatus.FINISHED`.
- **`JobInstance` = Job name + JobParameters; `JobExecution` = one run attempt** — re-running a failed job with the same parameters creates a new `JobExecution` for the existing `JobInstance`.
- **`@StepScope` enables late binding of job parameters** — required for readers and writers that depend on `@Value("#{jobParameters['x']}")`.
- **Chunk and Tasklet are mutually exclusive within a Step** — pick one; the builder API enforces this.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring Batch structures batch processing around a clear hierarchy: Job, Step, and either Chunk or Tasklet at the step level. Every layer is persisted to the JobRepository, which is what makes restart and audit possible.

**The hierarchy**
- **Job** — the overall batch process, like 'import monthly invoices'; composed of one or more Steps in sequence or conditionally
- **Step** — one phase of the job; each Step has its own execution status and can be restarted independently
- **Chunk** — the read-process-write model for a step; reads N items, processes each, writes the batch — all inside one transaction
- **Tasklet** — a single operation for a step; not a read-process-write loop; `execute()` returns `RepeatStatus.FINISHED`

**JobRepository — the persistence layer**
- Stores `JobInstance` (logical job run identified by Job name + JobParameters)
- Stores `JobExecution` (one physical attempt at the JobInstance)
- Stores `StepExecution` (per-step state plus serialized ExecutionContext for restart)
- Spring Boot auto-configures it from the application's `DataSource`

**Chunk transaction model**
- Chunk size 100 means: read 100 records, process each, write all 100 in one transaction
- A write failure rolls back only that chunk — already committed chunks are not re-processed on restart
- Larger chunks: fewer transactions, better throughput; smaller chunks: finer-grained checkpointing

**Tasklet vs Chunk**
- Chunk model is for streaming work — rows in a table, lines in a file
- Tasklet is for one-shot work — truncating a table, sending a notification, calling a stored procedure
- They are mutually exclusive within a single Step

In an interview, I'd emphasize the JobRepository — most candidates skip it, but it's what makes Spring Batch suitable for production rather than a hand-rolled loop.

questions.question: When should you reach for Spring Batch versus plain JDBC batch updates with PreparedStatement.addBatch()? What does Spring Batch actually buy you?
questions.title: Spring Batch vs Plain JDBC Batch — When the Framework Earns Its Weight
questions.direct_answer: Plain **JDBC `PreparedStatement.addBatch()`** is the right tool when the job is a single SQL statement repeated N times inside one process and you don't need restart, audit, or skip/retry. Spring Batch earns its weight when you need **restartability from the last checkpoint**, a **JobRepository audit trail**, **skip and retry policies** for bad records and transient errors, **partitioning** for parallel scale, or composition of multiple steps with conditional flow. The rough rule: if your batch is under a few minutes, single-statement, and never fails — use plain JDBC. If it processes millions of records over hours and a midnight failure must resume at 7 AM rather than restart from zero — use Spring Batch.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can articulate the operational features Spring Batch provides beyond batched SQL, and when those features justify the complexity
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Reaching for Spring Batch for every batch task, including ones that are a single 30-second SQL statement — over-engineering
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Frame the decision as restart-and-resume capability vs raw throughput — and mention that plain JDBC is often faster per-row because it avoids the JobRepository writes

sections.title: Spring Batch Is Not Faster Than JDBC — It's More Recoverable
sections.content:
A surprising number of teams adopt Spring Batch expecting performance gains and discover the framework is actually **slower per row** than `PreparedStatement.addBatch()`.
- The framework adds JobRepository writes (a few SQL inserts per chunk for `BATCH_STEP_EXECUTION` updates), serialized ExecutionContext snapshots, and listener invocations.
- For a one-shot 30-second `INSERT ... SELECT` to copy a table, plain JDBC will always win on raw speed.

**The value Spring Batch delivers** is operational, not algorithmic.
- **Restartability** lets a job that fails at 7 million of 10 million records resume at 7 million on the next launch.
- **Skip and retry** policies handle bad rows and transient infrastructure errors without aborting the entire job.
- **Partitioning** scales work across threads or worker JVMs with per-partition restart semantics.
- **Audit metadata** in the BATCH tables shows exactly what ran, when, with which parameters, and how many records were processed — essential for compliance in regulated industries.

The interview-relevant framing: **plain JDBC for short, single-statement, low-stakes work; Spring Batch when the operational features pay for the overhead.** A 6-hour nightly ETL processing 50 million rows from a flat file into a partitioned warehouse table — Spring Batch every time. A 10-second `DELETE FROM staging WHERE created < NOW() - INTERVAL '7 days'` — `JdbcTemplate.execute()` is fine.

sections.title: Plain JDBC Batch vs Spring Batch — Feature by Feature
sections.content:
The decision comes down to which operational features you actually need.

| Capability | Plain JDBC `addBatch()` | Spring Batch |
|---|---|---|
| Raw throughput per row | Highest (no framework overhead) | Slightly slower (JobRepository writes) |
| Restart from last checkpoint | No — full re-run on failure | Yes — resumes at last committed chunk |
| Skip bad records with limit | Manual try/catch per row | `faultTolerant().skip(X.class).skipLimit(N)` |
| Retry transient errors | Manual loop with backoff | `retry(X.class).retryLimit(N).backOffPolicy(...)` |
| Audit trail of every run | None unless you build it | BATCH_JOB_EXECUTION + BATCH_STEP_EXECUTION |
| Parallel partitioning | Roll your own thread pool | `PartitionHandler` with grid size |
| Conditional step flow | None | `JobBuilder.start(a).on("FAILED").to(b).from(a).on("*").to(c)` |
| Idempotency protection | None | `JobInstanceAlreadyCompleteException` if same params |
| Parameter management | Method arguments | `JobParameters` persisted with every execution |
| Code lines for trivial job | 30 | 150 |
| Code lines for complex job | 2000+ (re-implementing the framework) | 400 (using the framework) |

sections.title: When Plain JDBC Batch Is the Right Answer — and What Good Code Looks Like
When Spring Batch Earns Its Weight — Concrete Production Scenarios
sections.content:
Spring Batch's value compounds with job duration, dataset size, and the cost of a partial failure. The five scenarios below are where the framework consistently pays back the learning curve.

**Scenario 1: Multi-hour ETL with restart requirement**
- Job runs 4 hours processing 50M rows from a flat file into a warehouse
- Failure at hour 3 must resume at the last committed chunk, not restart from zero
- Spring Batch saves 3 hours per failure; over a year of operations this is the dominant ROI

**Scenario 2: Dirty data with skip-and-continue requirements**
- Input contains malformed rows, validation failures, foreign-key violations
- Business requirement: skip bad rows up to a tolerance, log them to a dead-letter file, continue
- Spring Batch's `faultTolerant().skip(X.class).skipLimit(N).listener(skipListener)` is one builder chain
- Hand-rolled equivalent: per-row try/catch, counter, dead-letter writer, single-item recovery loop after batch failures

**Scenario 3: Audit and compliance requirements**
- Regulators or internal compliance need to see exactly what ran when, with what parameters, and how many records were processed
- BATCH_JOB_EXECUTION and BATCH_STEP_EXECUTION are the audit trail — query them, dashboard them
- Plain JDBC requires you to build this audit infrastructure yourself

**Scenario 4: Parallel partitioning for scale**
- 100M rows must process in 30 minutes; single-threaded throughput is 2 hours
- Spring Batch partitioner splits by `customer_id mod 16`; 16 worker steps run in parallel
- Each worker has its own restart state — only failed partitions re-run
- Hand-rolled equivalent is a thread pool, manual range splitting, manual checkpoint tracking

**Scenario 5: Composed jobs with conditional flow**
- Step 1 validates input; if it fails, Step 2 sends an alert and exits
- If Step 1 succeeds, Step 2 imports; on success, Step 3 archives the input file
- `JobBuilder.start(validate).on("FAILED").to(alert).from(validate).on("*").to(import).next(archive).end().build()`
- The DSL captures the flow declaratively; hand-rolled equivalent is nested if/else with state tracking

```java
@Bean
public Job orderJob(JobRepository repo, Step validate, Step alert, Step doImport, Step archive) {
    return new JobBuilder("orderJob", repo)
            .incrementer(new RunIdIncrementer())
            .start(validate)
                .on("FAILED").to(alert)
            .from(validate)
                .on("*").to(doImport)
            .next(archive)
            .end()
            .build();
}
```

sections.title: Plain JDBC vs Spring Batch — Honest Trade-Offs
sections.content:
Neither approach dominates. Each is the right answer for a different shape of work.

**When plain JDBC helps:**
- The job is a single SQL statement (or a few) repeated over a known dataset
- Failure cost is low — re-running from scratch is acceptable
- Total runtime is short enough that restart-from-zero is cheap
- You want absolute maximum throughput per row with no framework overhead
- The team is small and Spring Batch's learning curve outweighs the operational features

**When Spring Batch helps:**
- Total runtime exceeds 30 minutes and partial failure must not waste the previous work
- The job has multiple steps with conditional flow (validate → import → archive → notify)
- Audit trail of every run is a regulatory or operational requirement
- Skip-bad-records and retry-transient-errors logic would otherwise be hand-rolled per job
- Parallel partitioning is needed and you don't want to write the orchestration yourself

**Watch for:**
- **Adopting Spring Batch for trivial work** — a 10-second cleanup tasklet wrapped in JobRepository overhead is over-engineering
- **Sticking with plain JDBC past the inflection point** — every team that says 'we'll add restart later' ends up rebuilding 70% of Spring Batch poorly
- **Forgetting the JobRepository database overhead** — Spring Batch writes to BATCH_* tables on every step boundary; size your DB accordingly
- **Mixing both in the same codebase without convention** — pick one default per service so on-call doesn't have to learn two patterns

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Plain JDBC `PreparedStatement.addBatch()` is faster per row** — Spring Batch adds JobRepository overhead.
- **Spring Batch wins on operational features** — restart, skip, retry, audit, partitioning, conditional flow.
- **Restartability from the last committed chunk is the dominant ROI** — saves hours per failure on long-running jobs.
- **Skip and retry policies are one builder chain in Spring Batch** — hand-rolled equivalents are 200+ lines per job.
- **JobRepository BATCH_* tables are your audit trail** — query them for compliance, dashboard them for ops.
- **Use `JdbcTemplate.batchUpdate` for short single-statement work** — 30 lines of code for jobs under a few minutes.
- **Enable `rewriteBatchedStatements=true` (MySQL) or `reWriteBatchedInserts=true` (PostgreSQL)** — 5-10x throughput on insert-heavy batches.
- **The decision rule** — under 30 minutes, single statement, low stakes = plain JDBC; multi-hour, multi-step, must-resume = Spring Batch.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Plain JDBC and Spring Batch solve different problems. Plain JDBC's `PreparedStatement.addBatch()` is the right tool when you have a single SQL statement to repeat N times and failure means 'just re-run it'. Spring Batch is what you reach for when restart, audit, and skip/retry are operational requirements.

**Plain JDBC wins on:**
- Raw throughput per row — no framework overhead
- Code surface — 30 lines for a trivial batch task
- Simplicity — no JobRepository tables, no JobLauncher, no scope annotations

**Spring Batch wins on:**
- **Restartability** — a job that fails at 7M of 10M records resumes at 7M, not 0
- **Skip and retry policies** — `faultTolerant().skip(ParseException.class).skipLimit(100).retry(TransientDataAccessException.class).retryLimit(3)` is one builder chain; hand-rolled equivalent is hundreds of lines
- **Audit trail** — BATCH_JOB_EXECUTION and BATCH_STEP_EXECUTION show every run, parameters, and counts
- **Partitioning** — declarative parallel scale with per-partition restart
- **Conditional flow** — `start(validate).on("FAILED").to(alert).from(validate).on("*").to(import)` is the DSL

**Decision rule I use:**
- Under 30 minutes, single statement, low stakes — plain JDBC with `JdbcTemplate.batchUpdate` plus the right DB driver flags
- Multi-hour, multi-step, must resume on failure — Spring Batch every time
- Adopting Spring Batch for trivial work is over-engineering; sticking with plain JDBC past the inflection point means rebuilding 70% of the framework poorly

In an interview, I'd lead with the framing that **Spring Batch is not faster — it's more recoverable**. Most candidates assume the framework brings performance; the real value is operational.
